title: TLS and Certificates with openssl
intro: Expired certificates, missing intermediate certs, and the wrong certificate served for a hostname cause a startling number of outages. openssl lets you see exactly what a server presents.

steps.prompt: Connect to api.example.com on port 443 and see the certificate chain the server presents.
steps.fake_output:
Certificate chain
 0 s:CN = api.example.com
   i:C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R11
 1 s:C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R11
   i:C = US, O = Internet Security Research Group, CN = ISRG Root X1
Verify return code: 0 (ok)
steps.explanation: The server sends its own cert (0) plus the intermediate (1). 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)' means the chain validates.
steps.why: Add -servername so the server knows which hostname you want (SNI) — servers hosting many sites pick the certificate based on it. Without it, you may be shown a different default cert and misdiagnose the problem.

steps.prompt: Check just the validity dates of the certificate the server presents.
expected_commands: openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com < /dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
echo | openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com | openssl x509 -noout -dates
steps.explanation: Valid until Nov 28 — about two months left.
steps.why: This one-liner is worth keeping in a monitoring script. Certificate expiry is completely predictable, which makes an expiry-caused outage one of the most avoidable incidents there is (see networking-incident-002).

steps.prompt: Inspect a certificate file on disk in full detail, including which hostnames it covers.
steps.fake_output:
Subject: CN = api.example.com
Issuer: C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R11
Validity
    Not After : Nov 28 08:12:03 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:api.example.com, DNS:www.api.example.com
steps.explanation: The Subject Alternative Name (SAN) list is what actually determines which hostnames the cert is valid for.
steps.why: Modern clients ignore the CN field and only check SANs. 'Certificate is valid but browsers say hostname mismatch' almost always means the hostname you're using isn't in this SAN list.

steps.prompt: Generate a new private key and a certificate signing request (CSR) to send to a certificate authority.
steps.fake_output:
Generating a RSA private key
.....+++++
writing new private key to 'key.pem'
Country Name (2 letter code) [AU]:US
Common Name (e.g. server FQDN) []:api.example.com
steps.explanation: key.pem is the private key (never leaves your server); csr.pem is what you submit to the CA.
steps.why: -nodes means the key isn't passphrase-protected, which is required for a web server to start unattended — so protect key.pem with file permissions (chmod 600) instead. In practice, ACME clients like certbot automate this whole flow for free certificates.

steps.prompt: A colleague suggests 'just use curl -k' to get past a certificate error. Run it to see what it does.
steps.explanation: -k skips ALL certificate verification — the request succeeds regardless of whether the cert is expired, self-signed, or belongs to someone else entirely.
steps.why: Fine for a one-off diagnostic ('is the app itself working, ignoring TLS?'), dangerous anywhere else. -k in a script or app config silently disables the protection against man-in-the-middle attacks — fix the certificate instead.
